stories.premise: The human asks for a job; the agent asks for a cap.

frames.caption: Safari, on the phone. Four presets, each already carrying a limit. Picking one only opens the next screen — nothing is issued here, and no prompt appears.
Still Safari. Every number is editable, which is the difference between a preset and a policy: the human changes what they mean, not what we chose.
The read-back comes first: what is being granted, in numbers, before any biometric. Only then does iOS draw its own sheet with the Face ID glyph. We choose when it appears; we never draw it.
The pass is signed and handed to the Wallet app. After this screen the page holds nothing — the wallet does. This is a transition between two apps, and it is the step people miss.

stories.premise: Forty payments happen and the human sees none of them.

frames.caption: This list is the whole user-visible surface of an agent spending money. The human sees it when they go looking, which is the design and not an outage.
The agent receives the rule that fired and the numbers, then stops. A refusal that says only "outside policy" is a support ticket, not an answer.
The middle verdict: not a yes, not a no. It carries what was checked and — the part nobody else prints — what was not, including whether the seller delivers.

stories.premise: The limit is too low. The agent asks; the human taps.

frames.caption: Same tint, same mark, same name as the pass in the wallet — in this drawing the page is the pass with controls on it. The agent drafts every change; the human is the only one who can approve one. AP2 has a word for this screen: a Trusted Surface, a non-agentic interface that renders the mandate to the human.
One tap, and the wallet pass shows the new numbers. There is no second card to keep in sync.

stories.premise: One action, and the name comes off.

frames.caption: Revocation is a signed statement, not an edit: the pass is immutable, so stopping it is a second object that names the serial. A revocation that needs re-signing is one that gets lost in a queue.
The pass keeps its place in the wallet and loses its colour and its claim. Nothing is deleted, so nothing can be quietly restored.
The misunderstanding worth a frame: removing the image from a phone changes nothing on the server. Only revocation changes what the endpoint says to a stranger.

stories.premise: Someone has never heard of us and wants one answer.

frames.caption: Each teammate gets its own cap and its own tint, and revoking one leaves the others alone.
A stranger scans the QR and lands on one page with one answer: active, revoked, expired or unknown. That page is /verify, and the link below is the page itself rather than a picture of it.

stories.premise: The cases nobody puts in a demo.

frames.caption: Fail closed, by design: an unreachable gate is not an approval. The alternative turns every outage into an unguarded spending window.
Nothing is issued, so there is nothing to spend and nothing to revoke. The agent learns why and stops.
The QR is the authority, not the picture. An old image is a claim about the past — which is also why a pass cannot be verified offline.
A caller must be able to tell "capped" from "broken". The body names the cap, says the service is working, and gives the reset.
